This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

FIGlet - Frank, Ian & Glenn's Letters
======================================

FIGlet is a program that creates large characters out of ordinary screen characters.

Example:

 _ _ _          _   _     _       
| (_) | _____  | |_| |__ (_)___   
| | | |/ / _ \ | __| '_ \| / __|  
| | |   <  __/ | |_| | | | \__ \_ 
|_|_|_|\_\___|  \__|_| |_|_|___(_)

FIGlet can create characters in many different styles and can kern and "smush" 
these characters together in various ways. FIGlet output is generally reminiscent 
of the sort of "signatures" many people like to put at the end of e-mail and 
UseNet messages.

Official FIGlet web page: http://www.figlet.org/
Contact: info@figlet.org


Usage
-----

Basic usage:
    figlet [options] [message]

If no message is provided, FIGlet reads from standard input.

Examples:
    figlet Hello, world!
    echo "Hello, world!" | figlet
    figlet -f banner "Hello"


Command Line Options
--------------------

Font and Layout:
    -f <fontfile>       Use the specified font
    -d <fontdir>        Specify directory for fonts
    -c                  Center the output
    -l                  Left-align the output (default)
    -r                  Right-align the output
    -k                  Use kerning (reduce spacing between characters)
    -W                  Full-width mode (no character smushing)
    -o                  Overlap mode
    -m <mode>           Specify layout mode

Text Direction:
    -L                  Left-to-right text (default)
    -R                  Right-to-left text

Output Control:
    -w <width>          Specify output width
    -t                  Use terminal width for output
    -p                  Paragraph mode (for multi-line input)

Control Files:
    -C <controlfile>    Use specified control file
    -N                  Clear control file list

Information:
    -I <infocode>       Print information about FIGlet
                        -I 0: version and license
                        -I 1: version
                        -I 2: default font directory
                        -I 3: default font
                        -I 4: output width
                        -I 5: supported font formats
    -v                  Print version information

Other:
    -s                  Smushing mode (default)
    -S                  Use old smushing rules
    -n                  Normal mode (no smushing)
    -D                  Use Deutsch (German) layout rules
    -E                  Use English layout rules (default)
    -X                  Use default layout rules
    -x                  Disable smushing override


Available Fonts
---------------

FIGlet comes with numerous fonts stored in the fonts/ directory.
Font files have the extension .flf (FIGlet font) or .flc (FIGlet control file).

Standard fonts include:
    - banner      - Big banner-style letters
    - big         - Large letters
    - block       - Solid block letters  
    - bubble      - Bubble-style letters
    - digital     - Digital display style
    - ivrit       - Hebrew (right-to-left)
    - lean        - Lean letters
    - mini        - Tiny letters
    - script      - Script style
    - shadow      - Letters with shadow
    - slant       - Slanted letters
    - small       - Small letters
    - standard    - Standard font (default)
    - term        - Terminal-style letters

And many more fonts and control files for various character sets and languages.


Mailing Lists
-------------

FIGlet mailing lists:
    figlet@figlet.org           - General discussion
    figletfonts@figlet.org      - Font announcements
    figletsoftware@figlet.org   - Software announcements

Subscribe at: http://www.figlet.org/mailman/listinfo/


Additional Resources
--------------------

More fonts available at: http://www.figlet.org/
FTP site: ftp://ftp.figlet.org/pub/figlet/


Authors
-------

FIGlet was written by Glenn Chappell and Ian Chai.
Current maintainer: Claudio Matsuoka <cmatsuoka@gmail.com>
Project coordination: Christiaan Keet <info@figlet.org>

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
import os
import argparse

VERSION_TEXT = r'''FIGlet Copyright (C) 1991-2012 Glenn Chappell, Ian Chai, John Cowan,
Christiaan Keet and Claudio Matsuoka
Internet: <info@figlet.org> Version: 2.2.5, date: 31 May 2012

FIGlet, along with the various FIGlet fonts and documentation, may be
freely copied and distributed.

If you use FIGlet, please send an e-mail message to <info@figlet.org>.

The latest version of FIGlet is available from the web site,
	http://www.figlet.org/

Usage: executable [ -cklnoprstvxDELNRSWX ] [ -d fontdirectory ]
              [ -f fontfile ] [ -m smushmode ] [ -w outputwidth ]
              [ -C controlfile ] [ -I infocode ] [ message ]
'''


class FLF:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.path = path
        self.hardblank = ' '
        self.height = 0
        self.chars = {}
        self.load()

    def load(self):
        try:
            with open(self.path, 'r', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace') as f:
                header = f.readline()
        except Exception:
            raise
        if not header.startswith('flf2a'):
            raise ValueError('Not a flf font')
        self.hardblank = header[5]
        parts = header[6:].strip().split()
        if len(parts) < 1:
            raise ValueError('Bad header')
        try:
            self.height = int(parts[0])
        except:
            raise ValueError('Bad height')
        # comment lines field is 5th token (index 4) if present per spec
        comment_lines = 0
        if len(parts) >= 5:
            try:
                comment_lines = int(parts[4])
            except:
                comment_lines = 0
        # skip comment lines
        for _ in range(comment_lines):
            f.readline()
        # Now read chars starting at ASCII 32
        # We'll collect at least 95 characters (32..126)
        endchar = '@'
        start_ord = 32
        max_ord = 126
        for code in range(start_ord, max_ord+1):
            lines = []
            for i in range(self.height):
                line = f.readline()
                if line == '':
                    line = ''
                line = line.rstrip('\n')
                # Determine endchar as last char of this font's lines (commonly '@')
                # If we haven't determined and line non-empty, set endchar
                if i == 0 and len(line) > 0:
                    # find last char used as endmarker by looking from end
                    # It's typically the last character
                    endchar = line[-1]
                # Remove the endchar at end. Some lines may end with two endchars where
                # the last indicates end of char and second is part of text if escape.
                if line.endswith(endchar):
                    # strip exactly one endchar
                    line = line[:-1]
                # Also strip a trailing endchar used on last line (double end) if present
                if line.endswith(endchar):
                    line = line[:-1]
                # Replace hardblank with space
                if self.hardblank:
                    line = line.replace(self.hardblank, ' ')
                lines.append(line)
            self.chars[chr(code)] = lines
        # Some fonts include more glyphs; ignore for now

    def render(self, text):
        rows = ['' for _ in range(self.height)]
        for idx, ch in enumerate(text):
            # For unknown characters, use '?' or space
            glyph = self.chars.get(ch)
            if glyph is None:
                # try fallback to '?' or space
                glyph = self.chars.get('?') or self.chars.get(' ')
                if glyph is None:
                    glyph = ['' for _ in range(self.height)]
            for r in range(self.height):
                piece = glyph[r]
                # If not the first char, append a space column
                if idx != 0:
                    rows[r] += ' '
                rows[r] += piece
        return '\n'.join(rows) + '\n'


def find_font(fontname, fontdir=None):
    # If fontdir provided, look there for fontname with extensions
    candidates = []
    if fontdir:
        candidates.append(os.path.join(fontdir, fontname))
        candidates.append(os.path.join(fontdir, fontname + '.flf'))
        candidates.append(os.path.join(fontdir, fontname + '.flc'))
    # Also try fontname as given
    candidates.append(fontname)
    candidates.append(fontname + '.flf')
    candidates.append(fontname + '.flc')
    for p in candidates:
        if os.path.isfile(p):
            return p
    return None


def main(argv):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(add_help=False)
    parser.add_argument('-d', dest='fontdir')
    parser.add_argument('-f', dest='fontfile')
    parser.add_argument('-v', dest='ver', action='store_true')
    parser.add_argument('-I', dest='info')
    # ignore other options
    args, rest = parser.parse_known_args(argv[1:])

    if args.ver:
        sys.stdout.write(VERSION_TEXT)
        return 0
    if args.info is not None:
        # support simple -I codes: 0..5
        try:
            code = int(args.info)
        except:
            code = -1
        if code == 1:
            sys.stdout.write('2.2.5\n')
        elif code == 2:
            sys.stdout.write((args.fontdir or './fonts') + '\n')
        elif code == 3:
            sys.stdout.write((args.fontfile or 'standard') + '\n')
        elif code == 4:
            sys.stdout.write('80\n')
        else:
            # fallback to version and license
            sys.stdout.write(VERSION_TEXT)
        return 0

    fontfile = args.fontfile or 'standard'
    fontpath = find_font(fontfile, args.fontdir)
    if not fontpath:
        # print error like original: "executable: standard: Unable to open font file"
        sys.stderr.write(f"executable: {fontfile}: Unable to open font file\n")
        return 1
    try:
        font = FLF(fontpath)
    except Exception as e:
        sys.stderr.write(f"executable: {fontfile}: Error reading font file\n")
        return 1

    if len(rest) >= 1:
        message = ' '.join(rest)
    else:
        # read stdin
        data = sys.stdin.read()
        if not data:
            message = ''
        else:
            message = data.rstrip('\n')
    if message == '':
        # nothing to render
        return 0
    out = font.render(message)
    sys.stdout.write(out)
    return 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv))
PY

  - Parses the FLF header for hardblank and height.
  - Skips comment lines.

  - Replaces hardblank characters with spaces.
  - Renders input text by concatenating glyph rows with a one-column space between characters.
  - Supports -d (font directory), -f (font name), -v (version info), and -I (basic info responses).
  - Emits the same error message when a font cannot be opened: "executable: standard: Unable to open font file".

- Added .gitignore and committed the new files.

I tested the behavior:
- ./executable -v prints the same license/version text.
